newsitem.title: YEMEN: Yemen may extend deadline for diplomat's release.
newsitem.headline: Yemen may extend deadline for diplomat's release.

text.p: Yemen said on Wednesday it might extend a midnight (2100 GMT) deadline for tribesmen to free a kidnapped French diplomat or face attack by security forces.

"If the deadline which we set ends and we need more time or a few hours until we settle the issue, we might extend it," Abdul-Wali al-Shumairi, governor of Marib province, told Reuters. He gave no further details.
Shumairi said he met the French ambassador and agreed that "any negotiations with the abductors have to go through local authorities and official channels".
"The ambassador assured me that the embassy will not carry out any negotiations with the hostage takers."
Security sources said earlier the tribesmen had asked to talk to officials from the French embassy to embarrass the Yemeni government.
The tribesmen from the Toaiman clan made their request to members of other tribes negotiating with them on behalf of the government.
"Talks with the abductors today seemed more serious...at the same time, the security forces are tightening the noose on the areas where abductors are staying," Shumairi said.
"Information available to us indicates that the diplomat is in good condition and is being looked after by the hostages".
The diplomat, seized on Monday as he drove his car in Sanaa, has not been named and French embassy officials have refused to comment.
He is being held in Marib province, 170 km (100 miles) north of the Yemeni capital.

The tribe is seeking government compensation for losses inflicted on homes, farms, water pumps and wells by floods which killed 65 people in June. It also wants more job opportunities and the settlement of a land dispute.
Authorities on Tuesday said security forces would attack homes of the Toaiman tribe if the diplomat was not released by Wednesday midnight.
Security officials said earlier they arrested 18 tribe members to put pressure on the abductors.
In recent years, tribes in Yemen with grievances against the government or foreign oil firms have kidnapped tourists or foreigners for use as bargaining chips.
At least two diplomats, an American and a Saudi ambassador, have been among the kidnap victims.
The tribes' demands have usually involved land or water issues, and have rarely been political. There have been no reported casualties from the abductions.
